q: How many Rotterdam criteria make the diagnosis of PCOS?
a: 2 of 3 (oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries), once other causes are excluded.

q: Ultrasound threshold for polycystic ovarian morphology on TVUS?
a: ≥ 20 follicles per ovary and/or ovarian volume ≥ 10 mL.

q: mFG score that defines hirsutism in the 2023 PCOS guideline?
a: 4–6 or more.

q: Why is SHBG low in PCOS?
a: Hyperinsulinaemia suppresses hepatic SHBG production, raising free testosterone.

q: Which blood test screens for non-classic CAH?
a: Early-morning, follicular-phase 17-hydroxyprogesterone (confirm with an ACTH stimulation test).

q: Which blood test can replace ultrasound for the ovarian criterion in adults?
a: Serum AMH.

q: Why isn't ultrasound used to diagnose PCOS within 8 years of menarche?
a: Multifollicular ovaries are normal at that age.

q: How does spironolactone reduce hirsutism, and why does it need contraception?
a: It blocks androgen receptors (and reduces androgen synthesis); it can feminise a male fetus.

q: Which antiandrogen carries a dose-dependent meningioma risk?
a: Cyproterone acetate.

q: Minimum trial of hormonal treatment before judging hirsutism response?
a: 6 months.

q: Main mechanism of metformin in PCOS?
a: Reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves insulin sensitivity, lowering insulin and androgens.

q: How long must the COCP be stopped before androgen testing?
a: At least 3 months.

q: Definition of infertility by time?
a: No pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected sex; 6 months if she is ≥ 35.

q: How does letrozole induce ovulation?
a: Aromatase inhibition lowers oestrogen, reducing negative feedback so FSH rises.

q: How does clomiphene induce ovulation, and what is its main downside?
a: It blocks hypothalamic oestrogen receptors so FSH rises; its anti-oestrogenic effect thins the endometrium and thickens cervical mucus.

q: PPCOS II: live birth rates with letrozole vs clomiphene?
Letrozole starting dose and cycle days?
a: 2.5 mg daily on days 3–7, increasing to a maximum of 7.5 mg.

q: Definition of clomiphene resistance?
a: No ovulation at 150 mg daily.

q: Mid-luteal progesterone level that confirms ovulation?
a: Above about 30 nmol/L, about 7 days before the expected period.

q: WHO 2021 lower limits for semen volume and sperm concentration?
a: 1.4 mL and 16 million/mL.

q: WHO 2021 lower limits for progressive motility and normal morphology?
a: 30% progressive motility; 4% normal forms.

q: What does AMH reflect, and what does it not predict?
a: Ovarian reserve (the antral follicle pool); it doesn't predict natural fertility.

q: Which gonadotrophin protocol is used for ovulation induction in PCOS?
a: Low-dose step-up FSH with ultrasound monitoring, cancelling if too many follicles grow.

q: Advantage and drawbacks of laparoscopic ovarian drilling?
a: No multiple-pregnancy or OHSS risk; drawbacks are surgery, adhesions and reduced ovarian reserve.

q: WHO classification of endometrial hyperplasia?
a: Hyperplasia without atypia, and atypical hyperplasia (EIN).

q: Risk of hyperplasia without atypia progressing to cancer?
a: Under 5% over 20 years.

q: First-line treatment for hyperplasia without atypia, and minimum duration?
a: LNG-IUS for at least 6 months.

q: Surveillance and discharge criteria for hyperplasia without atypia?
a: Biopsy at least every 6 months; discharge after 2 consecutive negative biopsies.

q: Concurrent endometrial cancer rate with atypical hyperplasia?
a: Up to about 40% (about 43% in GOG 167).

q: Biopsy interval for fertility-sparing treatment of atypical hyperplasia?
a: Every 3 months until 2 consecutive negative biopsies.

q: If she declines an LNG-IUS for hyperplasia without atypia, what do you use?
a: Continuous oral progestogen (MPA 10–20 mg or norethisterone 10–15 mg daily), not cyclical.

q: Who needs annual biopsies after discharge from hyperplasia surveillance?
a: Those at higher relapse risk: BMI ≥ 35 or treated with oral progestogens.

q: Standard and high-dose folic acid, and who needs the high dose?
a: 0.5 mg daily; 5 mg if BMI ≥ 30, diabetes, previous NTD or on antiepileptics.

q: Iodine supplement dose before and during pregnancy?
a: 150 µg daily.

q: After MMR or varicella vaccine, how long to avoid pregnancy?
a: 28 days.

q: Aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention: dose and timing?
a: 150 mg at night, started before 16 weeks and continued to 36 weeks.

q: Which smoking-cessation drugs should be avoided in pregnancy?
a: Varenicline and bupropion; NRT is acceptable.

q: Which conditions are covered by preconception carrier screening in Australia?
a: Cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy and fragile X.

q: Which antiepileptic should be avoided in women who may become pregnant?
a: Sodium valproate.

q: Key mediator of the capillary leak in OHSS?
a: VEGF from hCG-stimulated granulosa-lutein cells.

q: Early vs late OHSS: timing and driver?
a: Early within about 7 days of the trigger (the trigger's hCG); late ≥ 10 days (pregnancy hCG).

q: Haematocrit thresholds for severe and critical OHSS?
a: Severe > 0.45; critical > 0.55.

q: Biochemical markers of severe OHSS besides haematocrit?
a: Na < 135, K > 5, albumin < 35 g/L.

q: Why avoid NSAIDs in OHSS?
a: Risk of renal impairment in a hypovolaemic patient.

q: Why avoid diuretics in OHSS?
a: They worsen intravascular depletion and haemoconcentration, raising thrombosis and renal risk.

q: Single most effective OHSS prevention in an IVF cycle?
a: A GnRH agonist trigger in an antagonist cycle, with freeze-all.

q: How does cabergoline reduce OHSS risk?
a: As a dopamine agonist it blocks VEGF receptor-2 signalling, reducing vascular permeability.

q: OHSS thromboprophylaxis: dose and duration if pregnant?
a: Enoxaparin 40 mg daily, continued to the end of the first trimester.

q: Name three risk factors for OHSS.
a: Any three of: PCOS or high AMH, young age, many follicles or high oestradiol, previous OHSS, hCG trigger, pregnancy.

q: Objective definition of heavy menstrual bleeding?
a: Loss of more than 80 mL per cycle.

q: What does PALM-COEIN stand for?
a: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia; Coagulopathy, Ovulatory, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified.

q: Mechanism of tranexamic acid?
a: Antifibrinolytic: blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen.

q: How does mefenamic acid reduce menstrual loss?
a: COX inhibition lowers endometrial prostaglandins (it also eases dysmenorrhoea).

q: How does a GnRH agonist shrink fibroids?
a: After an initial flare, pituitary desensitisation produces a hypo-oestrogenic state.

q: FIGO fibroid types 0, 1 and 2?
a: 0 pedunculated intracavitary; 1 submucosal < 50% intramural; 2 submucosal ≥ 50% intramural.

q: Which fibroid degeneration causes pain in pregnancy, and how is it managed?
a: Red (carneous) degeneration, usually 2nd trimester; analgesia and supportive care.

q: What did the FEMME trial show?
a: Myomectomy gave better quality of life at 2 years than uterine artery embolisation.

q: What is post-embolisation syndrome?
a: Pain, fever, nausea and a raised WCC after UAE, without infection.

q: Which features raise suspicion of leiomyosarcoma?
a: Rapid growth, especially after menopause, and an irregular, heterogeneous mass on MRI.

q: Ferritin level indicating iron deficiency?
a: Below 30 µg/L.

q: Fluid deficit limits for hypotonic media such as glycine?
a: 1,000 mL; 750 mL if elderly or comorbid.

q: Fluid deficit limits for isotonic saline?
a: 2,500 mL; 1,500 mL if elderly or comorbid.

q: Why does monopolar resection need glycine or sorbitol rather than saline?
a: Saline conducts electricity and disperses the current; bipolar instruments can use saline.

q: Why does glycine overload cause visual disturbance and confusion?
a: Glycine is an inhibitory retinal neurotransmitter; hyponatraemia and ammonia from its metabolism cause encephalopathy.

q: Maximum rate of sodium correction in hyponatraemia?
a: 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours.

q: Perforation at hysteroscopy: when do you need a laparoscopy?
a: If energy or suction was used, or it is lateral or bleeding; a blunt fundal perforation can be observed.

q: Commonest cause of Asherman's syndrome?
a: Curettage of a recently pregnant uterus (postpartum or after miscarriage).

q: Gold-standard test for Asherman's syndrome?
a: Hysteroscopy.

q: How does vasopressin reduce bleeding at myomectomy, and what is its main danger?
a: V1-mediated vasoconstriction; intravascular injection causes bradycardia, hypertension or cardiac arrest.

q: Pre-op misoprostol for myomectomy: dose and timing?
a: 400 µg vaginally (or rectally) about 1 hour before surgery.

q: Risk of uterine rupture in pregnancy after myomectomy?
a: About 0.5–1%.

q: Risk of conversion to hysterectomy at myomectomy?
a: About 1%.

q: Where does the ureter pass relative to the cervix and uterine artery?
a: About 1.5–2 cm lateral to the cervix, under the uterine artery.

q: Downside of a pre-op GnRH agonist before myomectomy?
a: It blurs the cleavage plane and can hide small fibroids, raising recurrence.

q: How long to wait before conceiving after myomectomy?
a: About 3–6 months.

q: Why avoid posterior uterine incisions at myomectomy?
a: They cause more adhesions to bowel, tubes and ovaries.

q: Daily maintenance fluid and electrolytes (NICE)?
a: Water 25–30 mL/kg; Na, K and Cl about 1 mmol/kg each; glucose 50–100 g.

q: AXR finding that favours ileus over obstruction?
a: Gas throughout small and large bowel with no transition point.

q: When does an unrecognised thermal bowel injury usually present?
a: Several days later (often day 3–7), with peritonitis or sepsis.

q: What is the lethal triad of haemorrhage?
a: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy.

q: ATLS class III haemorrhage: blood loss and heart rate?
a: 30–40% of blood volume; HR 120–140 with falling BP.

q: Classic warning sign of wound dehiscence?
a: Serosanguinous discharge, usually around days 5–8.

q: Which electrolyte disturbance commonly prolongs ileus?
a: Hypokalaemia (also hypomagnesaemia and hyponatraemia).

q: Three common sites of ureteric injury at hysterectomy?
a: Pelvic brim (infundibulopelvic ligament), under the uterine artery, and the vaginal angle.

q: How do you confirm a suspected bladder injury during surgery?
a: Retrograde fill with dye such as methylene blue, ± cystoscopy.

q: Catheter duration after primary repair of a bladder dome injury?
a: About 7–14 days, often with a cystogram before removal.

q: How do you confirm leaking fluid is urine?
a: Its creatinine is far higher than serum creatinine.

q: Best imaging for a suspected ureteric injury?
a: CT urogram with a delayed excretory phase.

q: Repair for a distal (lower-third) ureteric injury?
a: Ureteroneocystostomy ± psoas hitch or Boari flap.

q: When and how does a vesicovaginal fistula after hysterectomy present?
a: About 1–3 weeks later, with continuous vaginal leakage of urine.

q: Bedside test for a vesicovaginal fistula?
a: Three-swab (tampon) test with dye instilled into the bladder.
